summary: For ages 10–11, develop flexible mental calculation for multiplication, large numbers and mixed-operation strings. Learners build a repertoire of strategies — partitioning, compensation, doubling/halving, derived facts, factorising — and learn to SELECT and EXPLAIN the most efficient route for the particular numbers, applying order of operations mentally and sanity-checking with estimation. The central objective is flexible, structure-seeking judgement and strategy talk, not running a written column algorithm in the head.
misconceptions: Attempting the formal WRITTEN algorithm in the head (carrying columns mentally) instead of using an efficient mental strategy — error-prone and slow.
Partitioning errors: multiplying only one part (45×8 → 40×8 = 320 and forgetting 5×8) — dropping a partial product.
Compensation without adjusting back (99×6 = 100×6 but forgetting to subtract 6).
Ignoring order of operations in mixed mental strings (doing 250×3+500 left-to-right differently).
Believing there is one 'right' mental method, so failing to pick the most efficient route for the particular numbers.

activities.title: Mental maths strategy workspace: split, compensate, derive
steps: Given 45 × 8, partition 45 into 40 and 5, multiply each part by 8 (40×8 = 320, 5×8 = 40), then recombine the partial products to reach 360.
Use compensation on 99 × 6: compute 100 × 6 = 600, then subtract the adjustment 6 to get 594 — stating both the rounding move and the adjust-back step.
Grow a derived-fact chain from a known core fact: from 6 × 4 reach 60 × 4, 6.5 × 4 and 12 × 4, saying how each relative is obtained.
Solve a mixed-operation string such as 250 × 3 + 500: multiply first (250 × 3 = 750), then add 500 to get 1250, stating the order used.
For at least one calculation, try two different strategies (e.g. partitioning vs doubling 45 three times) and judge which was more efficient for those numbers.
Before finalising, give a rough estimate (45 × 8 lies between 40 × 8 = 320 and 50 × 8 = 400, so around 360) and check the answer fits.
activities.insight: Mental calculation is about decomposing numbers flexibly using place value and the distributive/associative laws, leveraging known facts to reduce memory load, and choosing the route that suits the particular numbers — not visualising a column method.

activities.title: Explain and compare: strategy talk
steps: After solving a calculation mentally, explain aloud how it was worked out ('I did 40×8 then 5×8 and added them').
Compare your method with a different method for the same calculation (e.g. 'you doubled 45 three times') and decide which is more efficient and why.
Respond to prompts such as: 'How did you break up 45 × 8 to make it easier?', 'Could doubling help instead?', and 'In 250 × 3 + 500, which do you do first and why?'
Judge whether a proposed shortcut is valid and efficient for the given numbers, not just whether it reaches an answer.
activities.insight: Articulating and comparing methods makes efficiency and mathematical structure explicit and shareable, and builds the metacognition behind flexible choice — the real target beyond speed.

activities.title: Strategy reference and fluency practice
steps: Consult a worked reference showing partition, compensate and derive each worked once, with a note of when each is most useful, then apply the matching strategy to new calculations.
Complete fill-in-the-missing-partial items (e.g. 40×8 + __ = 360) to confirm all parts are tracked.
Match each calculation to its most efficient strategy and justify the match.
Practise derived-fact chains for fluency, timing optional, always stating the known fact the answer was derived from.
activities.insight: A reference of worked strategies plus targeted practice consolidates fluency and strategy-identification, provided the learner is actively producing or completing calculations rather than only recognising answers.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to do these in their head, saying their strategy aloud: 45 × 8, then 250 × 3 + 500. Watch whether they partition, compensate, or use derived facts — and whether they keep track of the parts mentally rather than reaching for a written method.
checkAnswer: 360 (e.g. 40×8 + 5×8 = 320 + 40; or 45×8 = 45×4×2 = 180×2). 1250 (250×3 = 750, + 500 = 1250). The teacher watches for a deliberate mental strategy — partitioning, doubling, or compensation — held together across steps, not a mentally-visualised column algorithm.
